title: Why Learn to Write in the Age of AI?
author: Austin Scholar
summary: The Austin Scholar newsletter argues that writing remains essential in the age of generative AI because writing is fundamentally a thinking tool, not merely a delivery mechanism for finished ideas. Drawing on 'writing-to-learn' research and a widely cited study linking student writing to improved critical thinking, the author contends that AI can produce polished text but cannot replicate the cognitive work of retrieval, elaboration, organization, and metacognition that happens while a person composes. The piece walks through each of these four mechanisms individually, explaining how writing forces retrieval from memory, builds schemas connecting new material to existing knowledge, and exposes the 'illusion of explanatory depth' that lets people believe they understand something better than they do. The author frames writing as a desirable difficulty: effortful and slower than passive review, which is precisely why it produces durable learning. The essay concludes that writing's role in education must transform rather than disappear, since AI can handle low-level recall and recognition but cannot substitute for the higher-order thinking that composing an argument requires.
points: A meta-analysis of 48 studies found that writing-to-learn programs reliably improve academic achievement, and a separate study found college biology students who wrote to explain course content significantly improved critical thinking versus a non-writing control group.
Writing forces retrieval practice: composing a sentence from memory without notes is a small act of self-testing that strengthens future recall more than rereading or highlighting.

Writing exposes the 'illusion of explanatory depth' -- the common false belief that we understand a concept better than we actually do, which only becomes visible when we try to explain it in writing.
The author frames writing as a 'desirable difficulty,' arguing that its slowness and effort are the mechanism, not a drawback: 'The effort is the learning; writing is thinking.'

Because AI can now handle the lowest two levels of Depth of Knowledge (recall and recognition), the argument is that writing instruction must shift toward the higher levels that AI cannot substitute for.
quotes: Schools often treat writing as the final step of learning: first you understand it, then you write it up. But in practice, writing is often the very thing that creates understanding.
So if a teenager asked me why they should bother to learn to write in the age of AI, I would tell them this: writing is thinking.

When you write about a topic from memory, you're forced to pull information out of your head rather than simply recognize it on a page. This kind of active retrieval strengthens memory significantly more than simply rereading or highlighting.

Psychologists have shown that most of us walk around with an "illusion of explanatory depth", which means that we feel like we understand things far better than we actually do, until we're asked to explain them.

Desirable difficulty, which describes conditions that slow learning down in the moment but make it stick far better in the long run, is the underlying idea behind all of these learning science concepts.

One study of a ten-week creative writing program found that students' critical thinking scores rose 25% while a matched control group barely moved, and other creative writing interventions have produced measurable gains in cognitive flexibility.
The first two levels of Depth of Knowledge (recall and recognition) are increasingly easy to outsource, since AI can summarize, restate, and recombine information quickly.
